title: Greedy
summary: Commit to the locally best choice when an exchange argument says it is safe.

parts.rule: A greedy method builds a solution by repeatedly taking the choice that looks best right now. It is correct only when a short proof — often an exchange argument — shows that a local pick never blocks a better global answer. Sort first when the greedy key is an order statistic such as earliest finish time. Without that proof, greedy is only a heuristic.
parts.why: Greedy code is short, so it is over-applied. Many problems look greedy yet need DP (non-canonical coin systems, some knapsacks). Saying "I need a known pattern or an exchange proof" separates a safe greedy from a hopeful one before you lock the algorithm in an interview.
parts.example: Interval scheduling: choose the compatible interval that ends soonest. Given (1,4), (2,3), (3,5), (0,6), sort by end to get (2,3), (1,4), (3,5), (0,6). Take (2,3). The next compatible is (3,5). Skip the others as overlaps. Selected size is 2. Exchange idea: any optimal set can swap in the earliest-finishing interval without losing cardinality. Coin counterexample: denominations 1, 3, 4 targeting 6 — pure greedy takes 4+1+1 (three coins) while 3+3 uses two. That system is unsafe for greedy; switch to DP. Another safe pattern: always merge the two shortest files first when minimizing total concatenation cost (Huffman-style).
parts.use: Apply greedy to earliest-finish interval selection, Huffman-style repeated merges, Dijkstra with non-negative weights, and coin systems already known to be canonical. Apply it when you can state the exchange argument in a sentence or two during the interview.
parts.refuse: Reject greedy when a tiny counterexample exists and optimality is required. Reject it for general coin change or knapsack without structure. Reject sorting by the wrong key (start time instead of finish time for interval selection). Reject greedy Dijkstra once negative edges appear.

body:
Rule. A greedy method builds a solution by repeatedly taking the choice that looks best right now. It is correct only when a short proof — often an exchange argument — shows that a local pick never blocks a better global answer. Sort first when the greedy key is an order statistic such as earliest finish time. Without that proof, greedy is only a heuristic.

Why it matters. Greedy code is short, so it is over-applied. Many problems look greedy yet need DP (non-canonical coin systems, some knapsacks). Saying "I need a known pattern or an exchange proof" separates a safe greedy from a hopeful one before you lock the algorithm in an interview.

Worked example. Interval scheduling: choose the compatible interval that ends soonest. Given (1,4), (2,3), (3,5), (0,6), sort by end to get (2,3), (1,4), (3,5), (0,6). Take (2,3). The next compatible is (3,5). Skip the others as overlaps. Selected size is 2. Exchange idea: any optimal set can swap in the earliest-finishing interval without losing cardinality. Coin counterexample: denominations 1, 3, 4 targeting 6 — pure greedy takes 4+1+1 (three coins) while 3+3 uses two. That system is unsafe for greedy; switch to DP. Another safe pattern: always merge the two shortest files first when minimizing total concatenation cost (Huffman-style).

[[diagram:local-pick]]

When to use. Apply greedy to earliest-finish interval selection, Huffman-style repeated merges, Dijkstra with non-negative weights, and coin systems already known to be canonical. Apply it when you can state the exchange argument in a sentence or two during the interview.

When to refuse. Reject greedy when a tiny counterexample exists and optimality is required. Reject it for general coin change or knapsack without structure. Reject sorting by the wrong key (start time instead of finish time for interval selection). Reject greedy Dijkstra once negative edges appear.
